input:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through as a vapour. In this study, two membranes are compared using a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C, with the comparison focusing on flux and the separation factor. Flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

The polymer membrane delivers a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 120. Its flux fell by 8% over 500 h, indicating that the higher throughput is not fully sustained over the test duration. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, delivers a lower flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 but a considerably higher separation factor of 420, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Overall, the comparison reveals a clear trade-off: the polymer membrane leads on flux, the zeolite membrane leads on selectivity, and only the zeolite holds its flux across the period tested, so the preferred option will ultimately depend on the duty for which the membrane is intended.

It is important to note that only one feed composition was tested, and that no test ran beyond 500 h. It should also be noted that flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane; in this study, the three are reported together, albeit at one composition and over one duration.
target:
Pervaporation separates a liquid mixture at a membrane: the feed contacts one side of the membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Two membranes are compared on an 85 wt% n-butanol feed in water at 60 °C, on flux and on the separation factor. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1); the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

The polymer membrane passes more mass and separates less sharply: flux 1.8 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120. Its flux fell 8% over 500 h, so the higher throughput is not held over the test duration. The zeolite membrane gives flux 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 420, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The contrast is therefore two-sided: the polymer leads on flux by a wide margin and loses on selectivity by a wider one, and only the zeolite holds its flux across the period tested. The stability comparison rests on the flux record alone: unchanged within measurement error is a statement about flux over the duration, not a statement that the separation factor held its value across the same period. Which property governs the choice depends on the duty the membrane is bought for, and the comparison supplies both figures rather than a ranking.

One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane; the three are reported together here, at one composition and over one duration.
